A suitor is someone — typically a man — who pursues another person romantically, with a serious intention of winning their love, often with the goal of marriage.

The key idea packed into this word is active, earnest pursuit. A suitor isn't just someone who likes another person from afar. He is someone who is doing something about it — expressing interest, spending time, trying to impress, and making his intentions known.

In its most traditional and widely recognised sense, a suitor is a man who formally courts a woman.

Imagine a young woman in a household. Several men admire her and wish to marry her. They visit her home, bring gifts, write letters, speak politely to her family, and try to show that they would make a good husband. Each of these men is her suitor.

Notice something important: the word implies that the pursuit is still ongoing. A suitor is in the middle of trying — he has not yet won the person over. The moment she accepts him and they marry, he is no longer called a suitor. He becomes her husband. So the word captures a specific phase — the phase of seeking, pursuing, and hoping.

This is why you'll often hear phrases like:

  • "She had many suitors." (Many men were competing for her attention.)
  • "He presented himself as a worthy suitor." (He tried to prove he deserved her love.)
  • "She rejected all her suitors." (She turned down everyone who pursued her.)
Tone and Register: When Is This Word Used?

This is an important thing to understand about "suitor" — it carries a formal, old-fashioned, or literary flavour. It is not the word people ordinarily use in casual, everyday conversation today. If a friend says, "I met a guy I like," nobody around her would naturally say, "Oh, so she has a suitor!" It would sound stiff or theatrical.

You are most likely to encounter "suitor" in:

  • Classic literature and historical novels — Jane Austen's books, for instance, are full of suitors.
  • Formal or elevated writing — journalism, essays, or any piece aiming for a dignified tone.
  • Fairy tales and period dramas — stories set in older times where formal courtship was the norm.
  • Humorous or ironic modern use — sometimes people use "suitor" today precisely because it sounds old-fashioned, to be playful or dramatic about dating. "She turned down yet another suitor," said with a smile, is funny because of that contrast.

In the world of business and finance, "suitor" takes on a secondary but well-established meaning. Here, a suitor is a company or individual that is trying to acquire, buy out, or merge with another company.

Just as a romantic suitor pursues a person with the hope of joining their life, a business suitor pursues a company with the hope of joining — or absorbing — it.

For example:

  • "The struggling firm attracted several suitors who wanted to acquire it."
  • "The tech giant emerged as the most aggressive suitor in the bidding war."

The logic of the metaphor is perfect: in both cases, one party is seeking, and the other party has the power to accept or reject.

In a much older and now largely archaic legal sense, a "suitor" simply meant a person who files or pursues a lawsuit — someone seeking justice or remedy in a court. This comes from the broader root meaning of "one who seeks something." You might still encounter this usage in legal history or very old texts, but it is not part of everyday legal language today. It is worth knowing so you aren't confused if you come across it.
The Big Picture: What All Meanings Share

Whether romantic, business-related, or legal, every use of "suitor" shares one central thread:

A suitor is someone who is actively seeking something from another — and who has not yet obtained it.

The word always implies a kind of earnest, often competitive pursuit, and always from the position of someone who is hoping, trying, and waiting for a response.

"The princess's suitors gathered from across the kingdom."Men pursuing her for marriage
"She was charmed by the most persistent of her suitors."The man who kept courting her
"Three suitors made offers to purchase the company."Companies trying to acquire it
"He called himself her suitor, though she barely knew his name."Used with gentle irony

A suitor is a person — most classically a man — who is earnestly and actively pursuing someone (or something) in hopes of winning them over, most often in a romantic or marriage context, but also in business (acquisition) and rarely in law (a litigant). The word feels formal and somewhat old-fashioned, which gives it a literary, dignified, or occasionally humorous quality in modern usage. It describes someone in the middle of a pursuit — seeking, but not yet having succeeded.
